text: Lesson 1 covered how Dockerfile instructions become cached, cumulative layers. This lesson is about using that mechanic on purpose — because the order you write instructions in, what you put in a single RUN, and which base image tag you pin, are the three biggest levers on how fast your builds run and how small the image that ships actually is.

Before any instruction runs, Docker packages your whole build directory into a build context and sends it to the daemon. A .dockerignore file, same syntax as .gitignore, keeps that lean — excluding .git history, node_modules, and build artifacts that your Dockerfile never even references, so a stray file changing between builds can't accidentally invalidate a layer's cache for no reason.

Because a cache miss on one instruction invalidates every layer after it, order what changes rarely near the top of the Dockerfile, and what changes constantly near the bottom. The base image almost never changes. The dependency manifest changes occasionally. Application source changes on every commit — so it belongs last, not first.

Copy full source before running npm ci, and every code change invalidates that COPY layer, which invalidates npm ci right behind it — a full dependency reinstall on every single build. Copy just package.json and package-lock.json first, run npm ci, then copy the rest, and that install layer only reruns when the dependency manifest itself actually changes.

Layers are cumulative, so cleanup in a later RUN can't remove bytes an earlier RUN already committed — that apt package cache is still sitting in the install layer regardless. Chain install and cleanup together with && inside one RUN instead, and the temporary files never get baked into a committed layer in the first place.

Trimmed context, cache-friendly ordering, layer-local cleanup, and a deliberately pinned base image — node:20.17.0-slim, not the unqualified node:latest — are what separate a Dockerfile that rebuilds in seconds from one that reinstalls the world every time. Next lesson adds the other major lever: multi-stage builds, which keep your entire compiler toolchain out of the image that actually ships.
